items.title: Nails on roads
items.text: Ontario police officers in West Nipissing, Canada, are currently investigating multiple reports of roofing nails being deliberately dumped onto local roads and highways. Authorities warn that these scattered nails pose a serious safety hazard to drivers, as they can trigger sudden tire blowouts and cause motorists to lose control of their vehicles at high speeds. Beyond the immediate risk of dangerous road accidents, drivers also face unexpected financial costs from having to repair or replace punctured tires. Because the incidents appear to be intentional acts of vandalism or endangerment, investigators are treating the matter with urgency and working to identify those responsible. Police are urging residents, commuters, and anyone who may have witnessed suspicious activity along the affected routes or who has relevant dashcam footage or information regarding previous incidents to come forward and contact police immediately. Difficult words: blowout (a sudden loss of air pressure from a tire while driving), vandalism (deliberate destruction of or damage to public or private property), suspicious (seeming to involve criminality or wrongdoing). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Nails on roads
items.text: Police in a town in Canada are investigating reports that someone is purposely throwing roofing nails onto local roads and highways. Officers warn drivers that these sharp nails are a major safety danger because they can cause sudden flat tires and make drivers lose control of their cars. Also, damaged tires cost drivers a lot of money to repair or replace. Investigators believe the nails were left on the roads purposely and are trying to find out who did it. Police are asking anyone who saw someone dumping nails or has helpful information about past incidents to call them right away so they can keep the roads safe for everyone. Difficult words: purposely (done with a plan or doing it rather than by accident or mistake), roofing nail (a short nail used mainly for constructing roofs), dump (to drop something in a careless or untidy way). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Nails on roads
items.text: Police in a town in Canada are looking into a big problem on local roads and highways . Someone is throwing sharp nails onto the streets. Police say that these nails are very dangerous. They can break car tires and cause bad accidents. Repairing or buying new tires also costs a lot of money for drivers. Officers want to find the person who is doing this. Officers are asking people for help. Someone may have a camera in their car or other important information. The roads must be safe again. Difficult words: highway (a big road for fast travel), sharp (with a point which can cut you easily), tire (a rubber ring around a wheel of a car). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Good news of November
items.text: A recent global review highlights significant positive environmental and technological developments around the world. Renewable energy reached a major milestone as global solar capacity hit three terawatts, and supplied about nine percent of worldwide electricity demand. In conservation, white rhinos have been successfully reintroduced to Mozambique to help control vegetation and prevent wildfires. They joined similar wildlife revivals such as orangutans in Sumatra and giant anteaters in Argentina. Furthermore, land-use emissions have fallen by roughly 32 percent since the 2000s due to reduced deforestation and natural forest regrowth, while the UK and Google launched a trial project that uses AI to reroute flights and reduce warming contrails . In healthcare and social policy, the US approved a new targeted medication for narcolepsy , and Portugal marked 25 years since decriminalizing personal drug use in favor of treatment and rehabilitation, and showed long-term success in lowering overdose deaths and HIV rates. Difficult words: vegetation (plants), revival (an improvement in the condition, strength, or numbers of something), contrail (a long, thin white cloud of ice crystals formed behind an aircraft flying at high altitudes), narcolepsy (a disorder that affects the brain’s ability to control sleep-wake cycles, and causes sudden daytime sleepiness). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Good news of November
items.text: A new report shares wonderful news about the environment, technology, and health from around the world. Solar power is growing rapidly and is providing clean electricity for millions of people. In nature conservation , white rhinos returned to Mozambique to help clear tall grass and protect against wildfires, while rescued orangutans and giant anteaters are successfully breeding in Sumatra and Argentina. Scientists also noted that global land-use emissions dropped significantly because fewer forests are being cut down. In aviation , a new project uses smart technology to change airplane routes and stop warming clouds in the sky. Finally, medical science celebrated a new treatment approved in the US for sleeping disorders, and Portugal celebrated 25 years of helping drug addicts with health care instead of sending them to prison. Difficult words: conservation (protecting animals, plants, and resources from loss), breed (to produce babies), aviation (flying), addict (a person who is dependent on a drug). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Good news of November
items.text: There is a lot of good news about our planet and science today. Solar energy is growing very fast. It now produces clean power for millions of people. Animals are also getting help. White rhinos are back in Mozambique to keep nature safe. Endangered orangutans and anteaters are growing in number. Scientists report that cutting down forests is slowing down . It is very good for the climate. In the sky, airplanes are trying new paths to stop making warming clouds. Doctors in the US approve a new medicine for sleep problems. In Portugal, they help sick people instead of putting them in prison. It brings great changes. Difficult words: endangered (when there is a high chance that an animal or plant species will die out), slow down (to become slower or less active), approve (to officially say yes). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: U.S. brings an end to production of one-cent coin
items.text: The United States has officially brought an end to the production of its one-cent coin. President Donald Trump signed the Common Cents Act on Friday. However, the coin will remain legal tender and continue circulating. The US Mint had actually stopped manufacturing the penny (the nickname for the coin) in November 2025. Businesses now have to round cash transactions up or down to the nearest five cents when exact change is unavailable. The decision to discontinue minting the penny was an economic one. In 2024, each coin cost 3.69 cents to produce. The bill's author, Lisa McClain, said: "This legislation will save $85 million per year by permanently ending penny production. It's common sense." The penny's history dates back to the founding years of the United States. Congress established the US Mint in 1792. The following year, the mint distributed more than 11,000 one-cent coins. The penny underwent numerous design changes. Early designs included an image of Liberty, a Native American chief's headdress, and an eagle. In 1909, it featured a portrait of former President Abraham Lincoln to commemorate the centenary of his birth. The last major redesign was in 2010. Rising manufacturing costs gradually undermined the coin's viability, consigning it to history. items.title: Grand Theft Auto 6 is released worldwide
items.text: Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6) has finally been released. Millions of video game fans worldwide are now playing it. They have waited 13 years for a new GTA game since the release of GTA 5. Gaming experts say the latest version could be the biggest entertainment release in history. It has already sold millions of copies, and it is set to make billions of dollars. Some fans are so excited that they are taking days off work or school to play it. An HR company in the UK said that workers in Britain booked around 83,000 days off because of the game. Many fans tried to make their games consoles think they lived in New Zealand by changing their region settings. They tried this so they could play the game earlier. GTA 6 has received excellent reviews for its high-quality, realistic graphics and exciting story. Players get to explore a huge world of crime and follow the lives of two criminals. However, many experts warn that the game is unsuitable for children under the age of 17. That is because it contains violence, killing, car theft, bad language, drugs, alcohol and sexual content. Media expert Jasmine Hood Miller said: "In GTA, players commit crimes, sometimes against ordinary people who did nothing wrong." She added: "GTA is a very well-made game that teens find fun to play." items.title: Wire upgrade at fault for grounding all US flights
items.text: Thousands of flights across the USA were grounded on Friday the 13th following a major communications failure in the country's air traffic control system. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop after problems with radar and communications equipment. More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air at the time. Thousands of flights were cancelled, leaving passengers stranded at airports nationwide. The problem was eventually traced to an overloaded router, possibly as a result of maintenance work to replace decades-old copper wires with fibre-optic cables. The FAA lifted the ground stop almost five hours later. Operations may take days to return to normal. The incident sparked widespread concern. Officials quickly reassured the public that it was not another 9/11. The US homeland security secretary said there had been no indication of a cyberattack or national security threat. He described the incident as a "telecommunications outage". Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the failure on outdated infrastructure. He said: "We have old switches and old routers. We use 1980s little copper lines." He added: "It's an old system that went down. It went down everywhere. It got overloaded." Duffy warned that systems would "continue to break" unless Congress allocated extra funds. He said: "I can't build things if I don't have money." items.title: France blames Iran for cyberattack on freezers
items.text: The French government has blamed Iran for a cyberattack on supermarket freezers and refrigerators across France. The attacks happened last month. They hit around 700 supermarkets and shops. Hackers took control of the cooling systems in the fridges and freezers. Temperatures increased to more than 50 degrees Celsius. Thousands of tons of frozen food melted. Stores had to throw the food away because it was no longer safe to eat. The French Foreign Minister said the attack was on a level never seen before. France believes an Iranian cyber unit carried out the attack. Iran has strongly denied it was involved in the attacks and blamed the French government for them. Security experts have warned that cyberattacks could be more dangerous in the future. Similar attacks have already affected other European countries. A French blood bank has also been hit. Fortunately, workers stopped the blood products from being damaged. Cybersecurity expert Gerome Billois stated: "At the moment, they are attacking easy equipment, but we should be prepared to see attacks on other systems like water or electricity." Weak computer security can let hackers attack places and services, such as hospitals, airports, public transport and banks. This can put people's lives in danger. European officials have said that a strong response is needed. Buy my 1,000 Ideas and Activities for Language Teachers eBook. items.title: Strict rules for students in South Korea
items.text: South Korea is introducing strict anti-cheating measures ahead of its national college entrance exam, where over 500,000 students compete for scores that shape their future universities, careers, and social standing. The government’s crackdown follows a major scandal in which the top scorer of a national tax accountant exam confessed to using a hidden camera, a smartphone, and generative AI to obtain answers. Officials are now targeting smart glasses and hidden recording devices, deploying specially trained supervisors across 1,300 test sites to inspect students’ eye wear, and warning that cheaters face criminal prosecution. Despite intense academic pressure and calls to delay the test, the education ministry refused to postpone it. However, analysts doubt whether basic steps like blocking public Wi-Fi will stop tech-savvy cheaters, and note that expensive private tutoring already creates an uneven playing field in South Korea’s highly competitive education system. Difficult words: crackdown (severe action taken by authorities to stop illegal or unwanted behavior), tech-savvy (well-informed about or proficient in the use of modern technology, especially computers and digital devices), uneven (not equal, fair, or balanced in opportunity, quality, or distribution). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Strict rules for students in South Korea
items.text: South Korea is adding strict new rules to stop cheating during its national college entrance exam . More than 500,000 students take this important test, which decides their future universities and jobs. Recently, a major scandal happened when the top student in a national tax exam admitted to using a hidden camera and AI to find the right answers. Because of this, trained supervisors at 1,300 test centers will carefully check students’ glasses for hidden cameras before the exam begins. The education minister warned that anyone caught cheating with smart glasses will face serious legal punishment . Although the government refused to delay the test, experts question whether these rules will work and point out that expensive private schools already make the test unfair for poorer students. Difficult words: entrance exam (an examination a student must pass to get to a school, college, or university), scandal (an action which many people consider wrong and they are angry about it), punishment (a penalty for breaking a rule or law). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Strict rules for students in South Korea
items.text: More than 500,000 students in South Korea are taking a very big test to enter university. The test is very important for their future jobs and lives. Recently, someone cheats on another big exam. The man uses a small hidden camera and AI to get answers. Now, the government wants to stop cheating with smart glasses. Special workers will check students’ glasses at all test centers before the test starts. The government says that cheaters will get into big trouble with the police. Some experts think it is still hard to stop high-tech cheating. Also, the school system is already unfair. Rich people pay for better schools. These students do better on the test. Difficult words: enter (to come or get into a place or institution), hidden (when you keep something away from other people and they cannot see it), rich (when you have a lot of money). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Chef fired for refusing to put pineapple on pizza
items.text: An Italian chef in Brisbane, Australia, has been fired for refusing to put pineapple on pizzas, among other reasons. He went to the Fair Work Commission to fight his dismissal, but failed to get his job back. The chef stated that topping pizzas with the tropical fruit was an "insult to his culture". He claimed he was sacked from a restaurant in May after repeatedly refusing his boss's instructions to make pineapple and ham pizzas for diners. His employer contended that the refusal was one of several workplace issues. The commission rejected the chef's application because it was submitted after the deadline. The chef has since found a job at another Italian restaurant. The question of whether pineapple belongs on pizza is a controversial one. It continues to divide public opinion. Pizza purists are aghast at the idea, but it is an established menu staple in many countries. The Hawaiian pizza was reportedly invented in Canada in 1962 after a chef used ham and pineapple as toppings. The restaurant owner expressed his opinion on it. He admitted that while the pizza was not his "absolute favourite," he would not "turn his nose up at it". Many restaurateurs insist that customers should be free to enjoy whatever ingredients and toppings they choose. items.title: Czechs protest to keep free TV and radio
items.text: Up to 400,000 people gathered at Letná Park in Prague, Czech Republic, on Sunday in what organizers call the largest demonstration since the 1989 Velvet Revolution. Protesters opposed Prime Minister Andrej Babiš’s government plan to abolish public license fees and fund Czech Television and Czech Radio directly from the state budget while cutting their funding by 15 percent. Critics and media experts warn that direct state financing gives politicians financial leverage over newsrooms and threatens editorial independence, and draw comparisons to government pressure on media in Hungary and Slovakia. The bill was pushed rapidly through parliament at 4:36 AM, just ahead of the November 17th anniversary, and it became a catalyst for wider anger against the ruling coalition’s approach to culture, defense, and democratic institutions. Babiš is facing intense public pressure, and he announced he would skip Velvet Revolution celebrations to ease tensions and signaled openness to a compromise funding model. Difficult words: abolish (to formally put an end to a system, practice, or institution), leverage (the power or ability to influence people, events, or decisions and get the outcome you want), catalyst (a person or event that quickly causes a big change or action).
